title: A ‘Budget for all’ | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 03:46
-     - 24

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake smiles during the presentation of Budget 2027 in Parliament yesterday

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake yesterday in Parliament presented Budget for 2027, touted by many as a ‘Budget for all,’ and the ‘best Budget’ by any recent Government.

While the Budget raises total spending by Rs. 624 billion to Rs. 7.9 trillion, it spreads the increase across investment, manufacturing, agriculture, renewable energy, ports, aviation, railways, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), women-led business, disability access, education, and digitalisation, alongside a cut in personal income tax.

The 81st Budget, his National People’s Power (NPP) Government’s third, carries over 80 expenditure proposals against about a dozen revenue measures, and sets out the trade-off in plain terms: the primary surplus falls to 2.3% of GDP, or Rs. 890 billion, from 3.6%, and revenue slides to 15.8% of GDP from 16.5%, below the Government’s own 16% floor.

“A country’s Budget is not just an accounting exercise,” Dissanayake said, reprising the formulation he used last year. “Our expectation is to make it a Budget that strengthens the production economy, protects small and medium-scale industrialists, makes room for investment, connects knowledge and technology to the economy through digital economic activities, protects the environment, and ensures social justice.”

Total revenue and grants are estimated at Rs. 6.2 trillion, up Rs. 199 billion on the revised 2026 figure of Rs. 5.98 trillion, with tax revenue at Rs. 5.7 trillion.

Expenditure rises to Rs. 7.9 trillion from Rs. 7.3 trillion, of which recurrent spending is Rs. 5.8 trillion, capital spending Rs. 2 trillion, or 5.12% of GDP, and interest Rs. 862 billion. The deficit widens to Rs. 1.75 trillion or 4.5% of GDP from Rs. 1.3 trillion and 3.7%, and gross borrowing to Rs. 3.8 billion, including Rs. 700 billion in foreign financing.

Primary expenditure climbs to 13.6% of GDP, which the President attributed to Cyclone Ditwah reconstruction, before reverting to 13% in 2028. The Budget confirms Rs. 500 billion in supplementary provision for the cyclone and carries Rs. 260 billion of it into next year.

The revenue measures are dominated by relief. The personal income tax free threshold rises to Rs. 162,500 a month from Rs. 150,000, the annual exemption to Rs. 1.95 million, bands are reset to 6%, 12%, 18%, 24%, 30%, and 36%, and maximum relief rises to Rs. 36,250 a month.

The measure amounts to a revenue loss of Rs. 16 billion. The Special Commodity Levy on imported sprats falls to Rs. 10 a kilogramme from Rs. 100, on dried fish to Rs. 10 from Rs. 302, and on sugar by Rs. 50 from 13 November. CESS is cut 25% on some 800 Harmonised System (HS) codes and phased out over two years at Rs. 10,000 million. The Ports and Airports Development Levy goes on paper and solar batteries, Value Added Tax (VAT) is exempted on books and periodicals at Rs. 2.9 billion, and the Tourism Development Levy is abolished.

Investment promotion is the largest single thrust. Board of Investment (BOI) enterprises committing at least $ 3 million in export manufacturing or tourism receive a 200% enhanced capital allowance, double the present rate. A Treasury-owned promotion company staffed by private sector and foreign professionals takes Rs. 1.5 billion, the National Single Window for Trade Rs. 2 billion, and Customs scanners Rs. 1 billion. A National Quality Infrastructure agency is to be formed.

Energy spending centres on grid stability, with Rs. 26. 5 billion for synchronous condensers at Habarana and Mannar and a STATCOM at Padukka, backed by the World Bank. Battery storage rises to 560 MW from 160 MW, rooftop solar with storage attracts Rs. 25,000 a kilowatt to 10 kilowatts at Rs. 3.5 billion overall, and the Kilinochchi to Habarana 400kV line takes Rs. 500 million with $ 150 million sought from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB). Wind and solar parks are planned at Mannar, Pooneryn, and Siyambalanduwa.

Ports take Rs. 24.2 billion. The West Container Terminal II is to be built to 3.2 million Twenty-Foot Equivalent Units (TEUs) with Asian Development Bank (ADB) and World Bank finance, a logistics centre goes to Request for Proposals (RFPs) within two months, and bunkering capacity grows by 50,000 cubic metres on build-operate-transfer terms. Trincomalee gets Rs. 1.3 billion and the Kankesanthurai passenger terminal Rs. 2 billion. At Katunayake, Terminal 1 expands to 9 million passengers at Rs. 15 billion with the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), while Mattala, carrying accumulated losses above Rs. 70 billion, is offered to international operators.

Rail electrification takes Rs. 80 billion million for the Kelani Valley, Main and Coastal lines, plus Rs. 1.2 billion million for the project. Roads absorb Rs. 487 billion, including Rs. 53.5 billion for Kadawatha to Meerigama and Rs. 30 billion for Nittambuwa to Pasyala.

MSMEs receive Rs. 67.7 billion in subsidised credit and guarantees expected to mobilise Rs. 174 billion in lending, with RE-MSME PLUS adding Rs. 20 billion at 5%. Women-headed households get group loans to Rs. 1 million at 3% through Samurdhi banks, with Rs. 200 million in seed subsidy and Rs. 12.5 billion in expected lending. Persons with disabilities get Rs. 150 million for assistive devices, Rs. 200 million for transport, and focal points in every Ministry. Allowances for the disabled, elderly, and kidney patients rise Rs. 2,500 to Rs. 12,500.

Education takes Rs. 278 billion, including Rs. 96.5 billion for a five-year digital program, and Mahapola rises to Rs. 20,000. Digitalisation is budgeted at Rs. 28.5 billion. Irrigation gets Rs. 77 billion, fertiliser Rs. 44 billion at Rs. 30,000 a hectare, northern fishing harbours Rs. 5 billion, and rural water Rs. 85 billion. Health takes Rs. 439 billion, including 6,534 new staff and Rs. 3 billion for ambulances.

President Dissanayake flagged El Niño, expected by the World Meteorological Organisation to peak in February 2027, as a risk to food and hydropower, and closed with a challenge to the Opposition. “Govern the Government. Question our policies. Produce a better program than ours,” he said, adding that the sacrifices borne through the crisis should not be made permanent.

title: Buddhist sermons from AKD amid Budget speech to Opposition on right path | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 03:45
-     - 12

Assuring the 2027 Budget focusses on prosperity for future generations, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake yesterday used sermons from Buddhism in Parliament to drive home the point how the Opposition should conduct itself.

In concluding his 2027 Budget presentation, Dissanayake said: “In the modern world, Governments are changed through progressive ideological revolutions, through the intelligent decisions of the people, and through advanced policies and programs suited to the future.

However, our Opposition is still clinging to superstitious beliefs and has been unable to free itself from regressive thinking.”

Politics, the President said, must be done by going among the people on the ground, not by tying threads in cemeteries at night, nor by wasting the time of Parliament reciting curse verses. “Likewise, read the Kalama Sutta, which the Lord Buddha preached to the Kalamas (the residents of the town of Kesaputta), pointing out that nothing should be accepted blindly but should be examined with wisdom, and understand the revolution the Lord Buddha made against blind faith. Read the Aggañña Sutta, which the Lord Buddha preached against superstition, and the Kevatta Sutta, preached against false incantations, and understand the ideological revolution brought about by the Lord Buddha,” the President said in Parliament. 

“In the Tevijja Sutta, the Lord Buddha asks whether, if a man standing on this bank of a river, wishing to go to the other bank, neither swims nor uses a boat but prays to the far bank, saying ‘Come here, far bank, come here,’ the far bank would come to this side,” Dissanayake added. 

“Criticise the Government. Question our policies. Present a better alternative program than ours. We fully accept your democratic right to do so. But bring alternative policies instead of curse verses, creative solutions instead of sorcery, and intelligent dialogue instead of Yaga and Homa rituals into the politics of this country,” the President emphasised amidst applause from Government benches.

“When the people of our country are moving forward with technology and intelligence, should the politics of the Opposition alone turn upside down and go backwards? I would like to remind at this moment that building a political culture that befits the civilised, enlightened and proud Sri Lankan identity we are trying to build before the world is a fundamental responsibility entrusted not only to the Government, but also to the Opposition. The intelligent people of this country will never again set foot in that old darkness. What we must leave behind for future generations is not our party disputes, but a prosperous and just country whose future they can take over with confidence,” stressed Dissanayake. 

Focusing on the 2027 Budget, the President said its proposals are not confined to paper alone. “They are proposals that are implemented in practice on the ground. Therefore, every new proposal will have a clearly accountable institution, outcome indicators, national priorities, a cash flow plan, and a transparency that can be easily observed by the public,” he said.

“What we are striving to build is a country that safeguards the dignity of the citizen, ensures the safety of the child, gives due value to labour, creates opportunities for knowledge, and protects natural resources for future generations,” he added. 

Having overcome the challenges that prevailed and built stability in the economy, the President said the Government’s next target is to commence a forward-looking and transformative era in 2027. “For this, the collective strength and contribution of all of you is essential to us. We have a very clear, progressive, and proud dream for our motherland. Our hope is to make this country not merely an island, but one of the most advanced countries, not only in Asia but in the whole world, rich in knowledge, skills, and modern technology,” he emphasised.

He said via 2027 budget, the Government is implementing a strong program towards that end. “We have commenced the transformation of making our younger generation and our children across the country fully skilled, advanced citizens by providing them with modern technology, science and global knowledge 

“What we need is not only to build an economically developed country, but also to build a new image of the Sri Lankan before the world. Our dream is to brand Sri Lanka in the world in such a way that a Sri Lankan is recognised as an educated, intelligent, civilised, respectable and trustworthy citizen. Our expectation is to mark before the world that, though we are a small country, our human resources are endowed with a unique intelligence. We want to prove to the whole world that we have a generation of citizens who fulfil the responsibilities they have undertaken, work with dedication, create new ideas, find solutions in the face of challenges, and can move forward shoulder to shoulder with the world. What we are trying to build is not only a new economy for Sri Lanka, but also a new recognition, a new respect and a new pride for the Sri Lankan before the world.

“Therefore, let us make the name ‘Sri Lankan’ not merely a name we pronounce with pride, but a proud name that the whole world accepts with respect. Let us prove our pledge towards that, not merely in words, but through action. Today, we extend an invitation with an open heart to all political parties in this country, to all stakeholders, and to every Sri Lankan living anywhere in the world. Come, let’s become partners in building the future of this country. We do not need to think along the same lines. We do not need to hold the same opinion. But our country is greater than our differences. The future of our children is more valuable than our individual goals. Therefore, let us bring together our knowledge, our abilities and our strengths. Let us begin from where we can agree. Let us unite, not to get ahead of one another, but to take our motherland ahead of us all! In the end, what we must leave behind for our children is not the story of how far above one another we stood, but the story of how high we all, together, raised this country.

“The victory of that story will not belong to one individual. It will not belong to one party. It will not belong to one generation alone. That victory will belong to every citizen of this country. That victory must have only one name – Sri Lanka,” the President stressed.

title: Five-day business name registrations now possible after 108-year system overhaul | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 03:38
-     - 17

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe (second from left) at the launch of the BNR platform

The pilot project of the simplified and Unified Business Name Registration (BNR) process, introduced with the aim of making business name registration in Sri Lanka simpler, more efficient and accessible, was officially launched on Tuesday in Anuradhapura by Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe.

Implemented through the collaboration of the Ministry, Chrysalis and the Provincial Councils, the initiative aims to simplify the registration process for sole proprietorships and partnerships while introducing a uniform system across the country.

Sri Lanka’s business name registration process has long operated under a legal framework dating back to 1918. The previous system involved complex administrative requirements, including the submission of land ownership documents and obtaining approvals from various government institutions.

Under the new reform, business name registration will be separated from the process of obtaining other regulatory licences and approvals required to operate a business. By introducing a simplified procedure based on essential identity and residential verification requirements, the initiative aims to facilitate business name registration within as little as five days.

As the first phase of implementation, a three-month pilot project will be conducted through 20 selected Divisional Secretariat Divisions across four provinces: Central, Northern, North Central and North Western.

Following an assessment of the pilot project’s progress, the Ministry plans to expand the new registration system island-wide. The initiative also includes plans to transition towards a digital platform in the coming years to further improve efficiency and accessibility.

The primary objective of this reform is to reduce administrative barriers faced by aspiring entrepreneurs and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), enabling them to enter the formal economy more easily and create a more supportive environment for starting and developing businesses.

The inaugural event was attended by Ministry Additional Secretary of the Anoja Herath, Director - Entrepreneurship Development Susanthi Jayasinghe; Director – Entrepreneurship Development Evangeline St. Clair, Chrysalis Chief Executive Officer Ashika Gunasekara, Senior Consultant Padmasiri Gunawardena, and Secretaries and officials of the provincial and divisional institutions involved

title: Vehicle registrations fall 12.1% in Oct. | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 03:36
-     - 13

Total vehicle registrations declined 12.1% month-on-month to 47,628 units in October from 54,214 in September, reflecting a broad-based contraction across most major vehicle categories, according to JB Securities.

Two-wheeler registrations fell 13% to 33,722 units, while motor car registrations declined 17.9% to 2,802. SUV and crossover registrations dropped 13.8% to 3,399 units. Pickup and commercial vehicle registrations also recorded declines. Electric vehicle registrations increased 5.4% to 6,374 units, supported mainly by electric two-wheelers, which rose to 5,342 units. Large tractor registrations also increased sharply by 49.1% to 407 units.

JB Securities CEO Murtaza Jafferjee said vehicle imports had reached $1.87 billion in the first nine months of 2026 and could total around $2.4 billion for the full year, approximately 20% above 2025 levels, if the prevailing monthly import rate continues. 

However, Jafferjee noted passenger vehicle imports have moderated amid the gradual exhaustion of pent-up demand, rupee depreciation, tighter credit conditions and higher import taxes. He cautioned that lower vehicle imports, particularly passenger cars, could moderate vehicle-related tax revenue and weigh on GDP growth in the second half of 2026, against a high base in the corresponding period last year.

title: Aitken Spence records strong 1H performance with PBT up 71% | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 04:34
-     - 18

Executive Chairperson and Interim Managing Director Stasshani Jayawardena

Drawing on the strength of its diversified portfolio, Aitken Spence PLC said yesterday it  recorded a Profit Before Tax (PBT) of Rs. 2.8 billion for the six months ended 30 September 2026, an increase of 71.4% over the corresponding period of the previous financial year.

Earnings before interest expenses, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased by 20.6% to Rs. 10.1 billion. Furthermore, the Group’s revenue for the period amounted to Rs. 41.7 billion, while the Profit After Tax (PAT) recorded a 229% increase to Rs. 1.4 billion. 

The Maritime and Freight Logistics sector remained a key contributor to Group earnings, recording PBT of Rs. 3.3 billion while the sector’s revenue saw a 20% increase to Rs. 9.5 billion. The performance was supported by stronger contributions across the maritime, integrated container operations and freight businesses, driven by higher volumes, improved freight rates and favourable market conditions. Both local and overseas airline segments fared well. The bunkering operation recorded a significant increase in profits during the period supported by higher oil prices. Overseas port operations  reported improved profitability with increased domestic and transshipment throughput. 

The Tourism sector recorded revenue of Rs. 26 billion during the period, while the sector result, a loss of Rs. 1.6 billion, was impacted by occupancy pressures and higher operating costs in the Maldives. Improved room rates provided some support, alongside stronger margins in Sri Lanka and growth in passenger volumes and contribution at Aitken Spence Travels.

The Strategic Investments sector recorded revenue of Rs. 5.3 billion, with PBT reflecting a loss of Rs. 326 million for the period. Power Generation was impacted by planned maintenance-related disruptions at the waste to energy plant and due to an overhaul being carried out at a hydro-power plant which was affected by cyclone Ditwah. Printing and Packaging recorded improved performance for the six months, while Plantations reported higher profitability, despite lower tea prices affecting second-quarter performance. The apparel segment continued to report losses with global economic challenges and productivity issues. As a strategic move the Group divested its equity interest in a subsidiary comprising three production facilities, after the balance sheet date. 

The Services sector recorded a PBT of Rs. 1.5 billion with a noteworthy increase of 179% and alongside a revenue of Rs. 998 million. The performance during the quarter was supported by Group’s equity-accounted Port City BPO venture which reported strong growth and gains from the disposal of an investment property during the period.

In a statement Aitken Spence said beyond financial performance, the Group continued to advance its sustainability strategy during the first half of the year prioritising impact control over energy, water, emissions, effluents, solid waste, resource and land use and ecosystem conservation. In addition to the Group’s effort to reduce direct emissions, a total of 97,994 MT metric tonnes of municipal solid waste was repurposed from the western province through the Group’s waste-to-energy operations, continuing the Group’s systemic contribution to keeping our cities clean. At other operations, 29,272 cubic meters (m3) of rainwater was harvested to support water security efforts. The Group continued to strengthen the systems and processes supporting its sustainability, climate resilience and disaster risk reduction programmes, while progressing its net-zero strategy.

During the second quarter of FY 2026/27, several notable developments took place across the Group’s portfolio. Aitken Spence Hotel Holdings PLC’s maiden listed, rated, unsecured, senior redeemable debenture issue, which opened on 15 September 2026, was fully subscribed on its opening day, attracting applications for the entire Rs. 5 billion on offer. The debentures were subsequently listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange in October.

In the Maldives, all five Aitken Spence Hotels properties secured Green Globe recertification, with each resort recording an improvement in its compliance score compared to 2024. Meanwhile, Rainforest Ecolodge, was recognised by the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority as the country’s first officially classified ecolodge and holding LEED Platinum certification, received Silver in the Nature Positive category at the ICRT Indian Subcontinent Awards 2026, recognising its contribution to responsible tourism, biodiversity conservation and community engagement.

Further recognition came through the Sri Lanka Sustainability Awards 2026, where Aitken Spence Logistics was named Sustainable Logistics Provider of the Year, acknowledging its integration of sustainability into its operations.

As part of its community engagement efforts, Aitken Spence Travels undertook the restoration of the library at Gangasiripura Kanishta Vidyalaya in Gampola, through its Pure Path sustainability platform and Nurturing Lilies programme, following damage caused by Cyclone Ditwah. The initiative has restored an important learning facility serving more than 1,400 students.

title: Liberty Lands and Developments unites diverse ventures under one vision | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 04:32
-     - 11

Liberty Lands and Developments (LLD), a diversified Sri Lankan business group with a legacy spanning over seven decades, has unveiled its unified corporate identity, bringing together its established presence across entertainment, hospitality, food and beverage, film distribution and audiovisual technology. 

The move marks a new chapter in the Group’s journey, reinforcing its commitment to introducing international standards and delivering quality experiences that enhance the everyday lives of Sri Lankans.

Guided by its corporate philosophy, “The Future, Built Right,” LLD remains focused on responsible growth, operational excellence and building businesses that serve future generations. As the Group strengthens its corporate presence, it aims to continue introducing globally inspired experiences while supporting local enterprise and contributing to Sri Lanka’s evolving commercial landscape.

Liberty Lands and Developments Chairman and Managing Director Imthiaz J. Cader said: “The foundation of our business was built on my father’s belief that success must come through honesty, hard work and the trust of the people we serve. As the second generation, our responsibility was not only to preserve what he established, but to strengthen the business and prepare it for the future. We have navigated many challenges over the decades, but our commitment to quality, integrity and long-term value has remained unchanged. Today, it is encouraging to see the next generation taking this legacy forward, introducing new ideas and expanding into sectors that contribute to the lives of Sri Lankans.”

The unveiling strengthens the corporate identity behind several established brands that have contributed to the country’s entertainment and lifestyle landscape. From pioneering cinema experiences to introducing contemporary dining concepts and advanced technology, LLD has progressively expanded into sectors that influence how people experience entertainment, hospitality and leisure.

The Group’s origins date back to 1955, when the late Jabir A. Cader established the iconic Liberty Cinema, laying the foundation for a business built on integrity, innovation and customer trust. Under the second-generation leadership of Imthiaz J. Cader, the business navigated significant changes in Sri Lanka’s economic and entertainment landscape, preserving its cinema heritage while establishing a stronger foundation for future expansion. His leadership was instrumental in the formal establishment of Liberty Lands and Developments in 1995, bringing its growing business interests under a common corporate structure. Across three generations, the Cader family has continued to build on this legacy, identifying opportunities to introduce new experiences to the Sri Lankan market.

Today, LLD’s entertainment presence is reflected through Scope Cinemas, which has transformed the local moviegoing experience by introducing premium cinema formats, advanced screening technologies and Sri Lanka’s first IMAX theatre. Complementing this, Liberty Cinemas and Next Frame Global continue to strengthen the Group’s involvement in international film distribution, connecting Sri Lankan audiences with major Hollywood studios and global releases.

In hospitality, LLD operates Ramada by Wyndham Colombo through Alhambra Hotels, offering accommodation, dining and event facilities backed by decades of industry experience. Its expansion into food and beverage through Food Studio has introduced contemporary dining destinations at leading shopping malls, bringing diverse international cuisines and home-grown culinary concepts closer to local consumers. Cine Digital extends the Group’s expertise into audiovisual technology, providing advanced cinema systems and integrated sound and visual solutions for commercial and hospitality environments.

title: Sri Lanka’s $ 5 b ICT/BPM export target by 2030 under spotlight | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 04:32
-     - 12

Sri Lanka’s aim to achieve its $ 5 billion ICT/BPM exports in terms of the National Export Development Plan (NEDP) 2026–2030 came under spotlight recently, at a high-level review involving the Export Development Board (EDB) and the Digital Economy Ministry officials.

The progress and challenges of Sri Lanka thus far on implementing the NEDP was discussed focusing on strengthening the contribution of the ICT/BPM sector towards achieving the country’s export growth ambitions. 

The meeting was chaired by Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne, Digital Economy Ministry Secretary G. G. S. C. Roshan, Chief Adviser to the President on Digital Economy and Information and Communication Technology Agency (ICTA) Chairman Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya, EDB Chairman Mangala Wijesinghe, Director General Erandika Dissanayake, EDB Additional Director General-Development Kumudinie Mudalige, and senior officials of GovTech and the EDB. 

The NEDP 2026–2030, formulated by the EDB under the guidance of the Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Ministry with technical assistance from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), serves as Sri Lanka’s national framework for advancing export development. The Plan sets an ambitious target of increasing total exports to $ 36 billion by 2030, including a dedicated target of $ 5 billion from digital products and services.

The discussion focused on identifying strategic interventions and strengthening the role of the Digital Economy Ministry and its affiliated institutions, including GovTech, as lead implementing agencies responsible for delivering key actions under the NEDP.

Among the key proposals discussed were identifying targeted interventions to achieve the $ 5 billion ICT export target through the Digital Products and Services Advisory Committee, establishing an effective mechanism to capture and monitor service sector export earnings, as well as addressing the foreign exchange conversion gap affecting the accurate measurement of service exports.

The discussion also highlighted the importance of introducing mandatory registration for exporters, and strengthening the inclusion of services in bilateral and regional trade agreements to improve international market access.

The meeting underscored the importance of strong institutional leadership, high-level policy intervention and coordinated action among relevant government institutions to accelerate the implementation of these strategic initiatives. The collaboration between the EDB, Digital Economy Ministry, GovTech and other relevant stakeholders is expected to play a pivotal role in strengthening Sri Lanka’s digital economy and expanding its footprint in international markets.

The EDB continues to engage with key Ministries and State agencies to facilitate the implementation of the NEDP 2026–2030, ensuring stronger inter-agency coordination, effective implementation of sectoral priorities and collective progress towards achieving national export target of $ 36 billion by 2030.

title: JXG, Ceylon Chamber launch new initiative to support entrepreneurs | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 04:29
-     - 12

From left: Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Senior Assistant Secretary General Manori Dissanayaka , Lead Consultant Dr. Nirmal De Silva, Secretary General/CEO Shiran Fernando, Chairperson Krishan Balendra,  JXG Founder and Chairman Emeritus C.T.A Schaffter, JXG Managing Director/Group CEO Ramesh Schaffter, Deputy CEO Dilshan Wirasekara and Chief Marketing Officer Gamika De Silva – Pic by Shehan Gunasekera

By Safna Malik

Janashakthi Group (JXG) and the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce have launched BREAKTHROUGH, a national entrepreneur development program aimed at identifying and supporting high-potential businesses across Sri Lanka through funding and business development support.

The program will cover all nine provinces and focus on two categories of applicants: existing businesses, including micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and startups operating in the manufacturing and services sectors.

A total of Rs. 70 million will be awarded to 20 selected businesses, with individual grants ranging from Rs. 1 million to Rs. 5 million. Applications will remain open  until 20 January 2027.

JXG Founder and Chairman Emeritus C.T.A. Schaffter said that the initiative seeks to help Sri Lankan entrepreneurs strengthen their businesses, expand their operations and realise their commercial potential. The launch comes as Sri Lanka seeks to accelerate private-sector growth, create employment opportunities and build more competitive enterprises. While several Sri Lankan companies have grown into globally recognised businesses, many entrepreneurs still face challenges in scaling their operations and accessing growth opportunities.

He also said that the name BREAKTHROUGH draws inspiration from the entrepreneurial journey of his business interests, which extended beyond insurance into sectors including dairy, manufacturing, exports, agriculture and education.

JXG Managing Director and Group CEO Ramesh Schaffter said the initiative was designed to provide entrepreneurs with practical support rather than simply recognise achievement.

“Do not count this as another awards ceremony. BREAKTHROUGH is about helping entrepreneurs build stronger businesses and equipping them with the resources, expertise and guidance needed to take the next step,” he said.

Reflecting on JXG’s legacy, he said successful businesses are often built by people willing to pursue opportunities beyond familiar boundaries and take calculated risks. He pointed to companies such as Expolanka, Virtusa and Vega Innovations as examples of Sri Lankan enterprises that began on a small scale before growing into significant ventures.

Schaffter said Sri Lanka has entrepreneurs with the ability to innovate, create jobs and contribute to economic development, and that JXG was committed to sharing its experience and professional expertise to help more local businesses realise that potential.

The initiative combines JXG’s experience in building and managing businesses with the Ceylon Chamber’s extensive network and institutional reach. The Chamber has also invited ecosystem partners to contribute expertise and resources to strengthen the program’s impact.

Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Secretary General and CEO Shiran Fernando said the growth of competitive enterprises would play a vital role in Sri Lanka’s economic progress and its ability to access wider local and international markets.

He welcomed the partnership with JXG and said BREAKTHROUGH would provide a structured platform to identify promising enterprises and support their development through financial assistance and year-long professional guidance.

“We believe this initiative can make a meaningful contribution to business growth, employment generation and the development of more competitive Sri Lankan enterprises,” Fernando said.

Speaking about the selection process, he said it will begin with provincial-level assessments, followed by workshops, mentoring and business development sessions for shortlisted applicants.

Final selections will be made by an expert panel based on business viability, innovation, scalability, sustainability, ethical practices and potential economic and community impact.

Funding allocations will be determined according to each business’s stage of development, growth objectives and funding requirements. Beyond the grants, the 20 selected businesses will participate in a structured 12-month post-award development program, gaining access to mentoring, investor networks, banking and insurance support, professional expertise and quarterly progress reviews.

JXG’s senior leadership and professionals from across the Group will contribute expertise in finance, human resources, information technology, marketing and legal services to help participating businesses strengthen governance, improve decision-making and prepare for sustainable growth.

Through BREAKTHROUGH, JXG and the Ceylon Chamber aim to make business development opportunities more accessible to entrepreneurs across the country and help promising enterprises translate ambition into long-term commercial success.

title: Oversight committee presses for EV, battery standards and stronger State research bodies | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 04:24
-     - 11

Parliament’s Sectoral Oversight Committee (SOC) on Science, Technology and Digital Transformation has called for mandatory regulations and standards for electric vehicles (EV) and battery technology, while also reviewing the performance of state research institutions and the commercialisation of innovations.

The committee met under the Chairmanship of MP Dr. Janaka Senarathna. It considered the 2022 Annual Report of the Sri Lanka National Engineering Research and Development Centre (NERDC), the 2023 Annual Report of the National Science and Technology Commission, the 2024 Annual Report of the Sri Lanka Inventors Commission, and the 2025 Annual Performance Report of the Science and Technology Ministry.

Members were told that NERDC has the capacity to test battery capacity, durability and lifespan, among other parameters. Officials warned, however, that no mandatory regulations or standards currently govern imported EVs, batteries, controllers and charging stations. 

They urged that relevant standards be set and that testing and certification be made compulsory.

The Committee also discussed the technology for converting fuel vehicles to electric, the need for training programs, and standards and regulatory mechanisms to ensure the safety of converted vehicles.

Officials flagged a shortage of human resources in research and development (R&D) institutions and called for suitable salary and allowance schemes to attract and retain qualified engineers and researchers. They also stressed the need to improve the performance of State research institutions, address shortcomings, manage research outcomes effectively and consolidate institutions with similar functions.

On the Inventors Commission, the Committee reviewed its electric fencing projects aimed at curbing the wild elephant threat, the setting up of university-affiliated incubation centres, and plans to promote innovation through digital platforms. Officials also said three of the four electric fencing projects implemented so far were operating successfully.

Members also discussed a proposal to amend the Intellectual Property Act to introduce a “Petty Patent system,” intended to protect inventors’ rights and speed up the commercialisation of inventions.

MPs Lasith Bashana Gamage, Chathura Galappaththi, Thanura Dissanayake, Hasara Liyanage and Chandima Hettiarachchi attended, along with officials of the Science and Technology Ministry.

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved submitting new regulations to Parliament approval aimed at strengthening disciplinary action against veterinary surgeons and veterinary practitioners found guilty of professional misconduct.

Under the proposed regulations, the Sri Lanka Veterinary Council will be empowered to issue warnings, temporarily suspend professional registration or cancel it altogether.

The regulations also define professional misconduct, abuse of office and other acts or omissions considered “infamous conduct” within the veterinary profession. They further set out procedures for appointing Boards of Inquiry to investigate allegations of misconduct involving veterinary professionals.

Formulated under the Veterinary Surgeons and Veterinary Practitioners Act, No. 46 of 1956, which provides the legal framework for registering veterinary professionals, determining their qualifications and regulating the profession, the rules were published as the Veterinary Surgeons and Veterinary Practitioners (Infamous Conduct) Regulations No. 1 of 2025. title: Customs rejects MP Nalin Bandara’s documentation  over seized drone consignment as CID launches probe | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 04:03
-     - 9

THE Customs has rejected follow-up documentation submitted by Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) Kurunegala District Parliamentarian Nalin Bandara Jayamaha regarding a consignment of 39 drones and 16 microphones seized at Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA) earlier this week. Simultaneously, the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has appointed a special team to investigate the unauthorized importation.

Customs officers intercepted the Parliamentarian on Sunday, November 8, at approximately 11:23 a.m. upon his arrival at BIA from Singapore aboard SriLankan Airlines flight UL 307. An inspection of his luggage uncovered 39 commercial camera drones—comprising DJI Lito X1, Lito 1, and Neo 2 models—alongside 16 DJI Mic Mini sets.

According to Customs Media Spokesperson Chandana Punchihewa, importing drones into Sri Lanka strictly requires three mandatory regulatory clearances:

n An Import Control Licence (ICL)

n Approval from the Telecommunications Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka (TRCSL)

n Clearance from the Ministry of Defence (MoD)

Following an initial notice, MP Bandara visited the Customs Department on Monday, November 9, to submit paperwork for the detained consignment. However, Punchihewa confirmed that officials could not accept the documents as legally valid approvals. Customs has issued the Parliamentarian a specific deadline to produce the required clearances, warning that formal legal action will be initiated under Customs regulations if he fails to comply.

Addressing the controversy, MP Bandara denied allegations of smuggling or tax evasion, maintaining that he declared the items upon arrival. He stated that the equipment was intended for a family-run camera drone rental and sales business operated by his wife and son, attributing the detention to incomplete Ministry of Defence paperwork.

Meanwhile, on the directives of Inspector General of Police Priyantha Weerasooriya, the matter has been referred to the CID. Police Media Spokesperson ASP F. U. Wootler confirmed that a dedicated team led by an Assistant Superintendent of Police has been appointed to conduct the criminal investigation, while the Ministry of Defence is expected to carry out a separate technical assessment of the seized devices.

title: The IMF, World Bank and ADB must reinvent themselves for a new world order | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 04:45
-     - 12

As highlighted recently at a webinar organised by the International Chamber of Commerce Sri Lanka and Daily FT , the world is changing at a pace that would have been difficult to imagine even a decade ago. By 2030, the global economic landscape could look fundamentally different, shaped by the emergence of new economic superpowers, shifting geopolitical alliances, wars, technological disruption and an unprecedented concentration of private wealth among a handful of entrepreneurs.

Against this backdrop, three of the most influential institutions in modern economic history — the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) — must seriously rethink their purpose, priorities and modus operandi.

For decades, these institutions have played a pivotal role in shaping the economic destinies and livelihoods of billions of people. They have provided financial assistance during crises, supported infrastructure development, strengthened institutions and helped countries navigate economic transitions. Their contribution to global development cannot be understated. However, past achievements cannot be a substitute for future relevance. The fundamental question is whether their traditional operating models are equipped to deal with a world that is rapidly moving beyond the economic and geopolitical assumptions on which these institutions were originally built.

The shifting balance of global power

By 2030, countries such as India, China, Indonesia and other emerging economies are likely to exercise considerably greater economic influence. The balance of global economic power is shifting, with Asia and the Global South demanding a stronger voice in international decision-making. Yet the governance structures, voting rights and leadership arrangements of these multilateral institutions have not always kept pace with these changes. Greater representation for emerging economies is no longer simply a question of fairness; it is essential for institutional legitimacy.

A new generation of world leaders and a changing geopolitical order

The geopolitical landscape is also changing, with a new generation of younger political leaders emerging across different regions. Their priorities and expectations are increasingly shaped by a different world order, where economic security, sustainability, climate resilience, poverty reduction, youth unemployment and social mobility are becoming central political concerns.

The IMF, World Bank and ADB must develop a much deeper understanding of these changing geopolitical realities. Geopolitics can no longer be viewed simply through the traditional lens of major-power rivalries, trade relationships and security alliances. It must also recognise the growing influence of the Global South, demographic change, resource security, technology and the aspirations of younger populations.

These emerging leaders will increasingly demand practical outcomes rather than policy prescriptions alone. They will want to know how international financing can create jobs, reduce poverty, protect the environment and improve education, support entrepreneurship and make their economies more resilient. Multilateral institutions that fail to understand these changing priorities risk losing their credibility and influence

The new development challenge: Jobs, youth, AI, wars and poverty

Perhaps the most compelling argument for reinvention emerged at the recent IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. World Bank President Ajay Banga highlighted a staggering demographic challenge: approximately 1.2 billion young people in developing economies will reach working age over the next 10 to 15 years, while current projections suggest that only around 400 million jobs will be created. This leaves a potential gap of approximately 800 million jobs.

This is more than an economic statistic. It is a potential social and economic crisis. Youth unemployment, underemployment and persistent poverty threaten social stability, economic inclusion and confidence in institutions. A generation without meaningful employment is a generation at risk of losing hope, dignity and the opportunity to participate productively in society. Banga made a powerful observation: a job is not simply a statistic; it represents dignity and the ability to build a future.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva also highlighted the disruptive implications of artificial intelligence, describing it as a slow-moving tsunami for the labour market. The IMF estimates that around 40% of jobs globally could be affected by AI through augmentation, transformation or displacement. Young people entering the workforce, particularly those seeking their first jobs, are especially exposed.

The implications are profound. Governments cannot continue to measure economic success solely through GDP growth, fiscal balances or debt sustainability. These remain essential, but growth that does not generate sufficient employment or reduce poverty risks becoming an increasingly fragile social contract.

The IMF, World Bank and ADB must therefore place job creation, human capital development, youth employability and poverty reduction much closer to the centre of their development strategies.

The growing influence of technology billionaires

Perhaps an even more profound development is the growing influence of technology billionaires and private capital. Individuals controlling global technology platforms, artificial intelligence ecosystems, digital payment networks and enormous pools of private wealth are increasingly capable of influencing global economic discussions.

Entrepreneurs such as Elon Musk and philanthropists such as Bill Gates demonstrate how individual wealth, technology and private initiatives can shape conversations on healthcare, education, energy, climate change and economic opportunity.

In some cases, these individuals command financial resources and technological capabilities that rival those of entire nations. Their ability to mobilise capital, make decisions and deploy solutions across borders can be considerably faster than the traditional processes of multilateral institutions. Will the future of development finance be determined as much by technology entrepreneurs and private philanthropists as by the IMF, World Bank and ADB?

The challenge for multilateral organisations is to engage these emerging centres of influence, mobilise their capital and technological capabilities, and ensure that development remains inclusive, transparent and accountable. Private wealth, with its ability to mobilise resources faster and deliver outcomes with less costs and bureaucracy, should complement — not replace — public institutions, democratic accountability and national sovereignty.

Technology: An opportunity and a threat

Artificial intelligence, automation, digital currencies, biotechnology and advances in healthcare will fundamentally change how economies function, how people work and how long they live.

At the recent Annual Meetings, Banga also emphasised the potential of practical, affordable AI applications to improve productivity in agriculture, healthcare, education and small businesses in developing economies. Georgieva highlighted the need for reliable electricity, digital infrastructure, appropriate skills and safeguards to ensure developing countries can participate in this transformation. However, technology also presents serious risks. Cyberattacks, digital vulnerabilities, data security and the concentration of technological power could expose governments, financial systems and multilateral institutions to new forms of systemic risk.

Digital platforms and financial technology could fundamentally change how development assistance reaches people. Instead of money passing through multiple layers of bureaucracy, technology could enable targeted funding, digital payments, healthcare services and educational opportunities to reach intended beneficiaries more directly. The institutions must help countries prepare for these transitions rather than simply respond after crises emerge. They must also ensure that AI becomes a tool for creating opportunities rather than widening the divide between those who possess technology and those who are left behind.

Gen Z

The next generation will bring different expectations. Gen Z is entering leadership positions across businesses, governments and institutions. They are digitally connected, globally aware and increasingly concerned about climate change, inequality, inclusion and economic opportunity. They will question traditional bureaucracies, slow decision-making and development models that fail to deliver tangible outcomes. Education systems must also move beyond qualifications towards practical skills, adaptability, entrepreneurship and lifelong learning. Public-private partnerships will be critical in creating pathways to first employment, particularly as AI changes traditional entry-level jobs.

Sri Lanka

For countries such as Sri Lanka, this transformation is particularly important. Assistance should go beyond stabilisation programs, debt restructuring and infrastructure financing. Countries need support in building competitive industries, attracting foreign direct investment, developing human capital, retaining talent and creating sustainable employment. Economic reforms must ultimately translate into better livelihoods, reduced poverty and improved living standards. Fiscal discipline and macroeconomic stability are indispensable, but they must create the foundation for productive investment and inclusive growth, not become ends in themselves.

The future

The IMF, World Bank and ADB should consider more agile financing mechanisms, faster project approvals, stronger private-sector partnerships and measurable development outcomes. They must become more proactive in anticipating sovereign debt risks, climate-related shocks, technological disruptions and demographic pressures. They should also collaborate more closely, reduce institutional duplication and leverage private capital, philanthropy and technology to deliver development outcomes at scale. The world of 2030 will not be the world of 1944, when the Bretton Woods institutions were conceived, or even 1966, when the ADB was established. With the US midterm elections now behind us, the world’s attention must return to these much bigger structural challenges. The institutions that helped shape the old world order must now help shape the new one. Their greatest challenge is no longer simply financing development. It is ensuring that economic growth creates jobs, that technology expands opportunity, countries have capacity to manage cyber risks, that poverty is reduced and that the next generation has a meaningful stake in the global economy. The next generation will not judge the IMF, World Bank and ADB by how effectively they manage debt crises or how much development finance they disburse, but by whether they can create jobs, reduce poverty, protect the planet and deliver a more equitable future. The ultimate measure of their success should not be how much money they lend, but how many lives they help transform and minimise world disasters and wars .

References

1. Ajay Banga, World Bank President – Remarks at the 2026 Annual Meetings Plenary, October 2026.

2. Kristalina Georgieva, IMF Managing Director – AI Will Transform the Global Economy. Let’s Make Sure It Benefits Humanity, IMF, January 2024.

3. World Bank Group – Small AI: More and Better Jobs, Annual Meetings 2026, Bangkok.

4. https://youtu.be/hIihN5By1C4?si=w3nId6CYhUgUc-

5.https://multilateralism.sipa.columbia.edu/news/multilateralism-not-dead-its-future-depends-how-knowledge-travels

title: Saqib steals the thunder on rain-affected day | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 03:20
-     - 7

Ground staff cover the pitch and surrounding areas at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium bringing an early end to Day 4

Saqib Khan picked up seven wickets on his Test debut to contain Sri Lanka

RAWALPINDI: There was only one full session of play on the fourth day of the first cricket Test between Sri Lanka and Pakistan and it belonged to just one man – Saqib Khan, who, on his Test debut, took seven wickets as Sri Lanka lost their last six wickets for 42 runs after resuming at 404-4 at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium yesterday.

Under overcast skies, Saqib came in with a plan and executed it to perfection. The debutant found the right areas to pick up his maiden fifer and ended up with figures of 7/130 to become the fourth Pakistani, after Mohammad Zahid, Mohammad Nazir, and Abrar Ahmed, to take 7 wickets in his debut innings, and the 19th bowler worldwide to achieve this remarkable feat.

Pakistan needed a strong morning session to stay alive in the contest and they delivered more than that, bowling Sri Lanka out for 446.

Saqib was the chief destroyer, claiming the first five wickets to fall in the morning. He struck in the very first over of the day to remove Dhananjaya de Silva without adding to his overnight score of 167, and soon accounted for the other centurion, Kusal Mendis, as well for 119. Sonal Dinusha offered some resistance, but Saqib eventually broke through his defence before adding two more wickets to complete a superb seven-wicket haul. His figures for the morning read 8-3-25-5. 

After struggling for consistency on Day 3, Saqib was right on the money yesterday and his spell ensured that Sri Lanka gained only a slender lead of just 12 runs in the first innings.

In their response, Pakistan’s batters looked solid, taking a lead of 45 before bad light followed by rain ended play for the day in a Test where already more than 100 overs have been lost. 

Asitha Fernando removed Tayyab Arif, but Azan Awais (22*) and Mohammad Thaha (24*) saw Pakistan through to 57-1. 

With only four sessions remaining, this Test is heading towards a certain draw.

title: SC determines two clauses in SLC Bill inconsistent and requires amendment | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 03:19
-     - 11

Speaker of Parliament Dr. Jagath Wickramaratne informed Parliament that the Supreme Court has determined that two clauses of the proposed Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) Bill are inconsistent with the Constitution and require a special majority for passage unless amended. 

Announcing the Supreme Court’s determination in Parliament, the Speaker said Clause 29 of the Bill infringes Article 14(1)(c) of the Constitution, while Clause 7(1) infringes Article 12(1).

Accordingly, the two clauses could be validly passed only with the special majority stipulated under Article 84(2) of the Constitution.

However, the Court has determined that these inconsistencies would cease if the amendments proposed by the Supreme Court are incorporated at the Committee Stage, enabling the Bill to be passed with a simple majority in Parliament.

The Supreme Court has further determined that, subject to these two clauses, none of the other provisions of the Bill is inconsistent with any provision of the Constitution.

The Speaker also ordered that the Supreme Court’s determination be included in the Official Report of Parliament’s proceedings.

title: FSL Chief apologises to nation following debacle against Bangladesh | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 13 November 2026 03:17
-     - 10

By Althaf Nawaz reporting from Dhaka, Bangladesh

Football Sri Lanka President Jaswar Umar

Football Sri Lanka President Jaswar Umar has apologised to the nation and the country’s passionate football fraternity following Sri Lanka’s disappointing exit from the SAFF Championship, while pledging to rebuild the national side and return stronger within the next eight months.

In a message aimed at restoring public confidence following the humiliating defeat at the hands of hosts Bangladesh, Umar acknowledged the disappointment of football fans who had pinned their hopes on seeing Sri Lanka reach the final. He admitted that the team had fallen short of expectations, but insisted that one disastrous outing should not overshadow the progress achieved during the ongoing rebuilding process.

Umar conceded that individual errors and the pressure of the occasion had contributed to Sri Lanka’s disappointing performance against Bangladesh. However, he maintained that the setback should be viewed in perspective, stressing that the national team had made considerable strides after emerging from one of the most challenging periods in the country’s football history.

Pointing to Sri Lanka’s improved standing in international football, the Football Sri Lanka chief highlighted the country’s climb from 207th to 184th in the FIFA World Rankings as evidence of the progress made under the rebuilding programme. He described the achievement as particularly significant, considering that Sri Lanka had remained above the 200th position for almost 15 years.

Umar further revealed that the national team had recorded 12 victories and six draws over the past two years, arguing that the recent defeat should not be allowed to erase the gains made during that period.

Calling for unity at a crucial juncture, he appealed to supporters not to abandon the team following its disappointing campaign, emphasising that genuine support for a national side must extend beyond victories and include moments of adversity.

“The SAFF Championship was an important milestone in our journey, but it was never the ultimate destination,” Umar maintained, underlining his commitment to bringing about sustainable and lasting improvements to Sri Lankan football.

In what could prove to be a significant development for the country’s football administration, Umar disclosed that discussions were already underway to explore the possibility of Sri Lanka hosting the next SAFF Championship, expected to be staged in approximately eight months.

He described the prospect of staging the regional showpiece on home soil as a major opportunity to revitalise the national team, reconnect with supporters and generate renewed enthusiasm for the sport across the country.

Umar also expressed confidence that football was once again capturing the attention of the public, pointing to the growing interest and national discussion surrounding the game. He acknowledged the contribution of the print, electronic, television and digital media in keeping the sport in the public spotlight and helping restore its popularity.

While conceding that much work remained to be done, the Football Sri Lanka President insisted that the latest setback would not derail his administration’s long-term plans. Instead, he pledged to address the shortcomings exposed during the tournament, strengthen the team’s foundations and work towards restoring Sri Lanka’s standing in regional football.

With the next SAFF Championship potentially just eight months away, Umar’s immediate challenge will be to translate his assurances into tangible results and ensure that the national team returns to the international stage with greater consistency, discipline and competitiveness.

His message to the nation was one of renewed determination: Sri Lankan football must learn from its failures, rebuild with purpose and return stronger.

The Old Nalandians Sports Club will host the 25th annual Col. Henry Steele Olcott Memorial Cricket Tournament at Nalanda College grounds from 13-15 November.

This Silver Jubilee edition coincides with the 30th anniversary of the Col. Henry Steele Olcott Memorial Foundation established in 1996. The event will bring together current and former cricketers from Olcott schools with an old girls’ friendly netball tournament also thrown in.

The Foundation was formed in 1996 by a committed group of past cricketers representing Olcott schools under the leadership of the late Bandula Warnapura, Sri Lanka first Test Captain. The inaugural tournament was held in 1999 organised by the Old Nalandians SC. Maliyadeva, Kurunegala emerged as the first tournament champions.

The tournament initially involved eight premier Buddhist schools – Ananda, Nalanda, Dharmaraja, Mahinda, Maliyadeva, Dharmasoka, Rahula Matara, and Dharmapala. Sri Rahula College, Katugastota and Vijaya College, Matale join this year bringing the number of participating schools to 10.

Old Nalandians SC is hosting this tournament for the fourth time having previously hosted it in 1999, 2007 and 2016. The Chief Guest on the final day will be distinguished Old Nalandian Thilanga Sumathipala.
